scenes.title: One box, three separate trials

beats.text: Consider a box at rest on a rough, level floor. We pull it horizontally to the right, in three separate trials.
In the first trial, a gentle pull leaves the box at rest.
Reset the box to rest for the second trial. A stronger pull brings it to the point of moving, but it still stays put.
Reset to rest again. In the third trial, a still stronger pull makes the box slide and speed up to the right.
Why does friction balance some pulls, but not all? Here are the details for all three trials.

scenes.text: Consider a box at rest on a rough, level floor. We pull it horizontally to the right, in three separate trials. In the first trial, a gentle pull leaves the box at rest. Reset the box to rest for the second trial. A stronger pull brings it to the point of moving, but it still stays put. Reset to rest again. In the third trial, a still stronger pull makes the box slide and speed up to the right. Why does friction balance some pulls but not all? Here are the details for all three trials.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The box has mass five kilograms.
The coefficient of friction between box and floor is zero point four.
Take g as ten metres per second squared.
The independent pulls are twelve newtons in trial A, twenty newtons in trial B, and twenty five newtons in trial C.
Each trial starts from rest on the rough horizontal floor. Contact is maintained, and each pull stays constant. Use the ideal model: sliding friction equals limiting friction.
Find the normal reaction and the limiting friction. Then find actual friction and acceleration in each trial. First, what does the coefficient tell us?

Contact is maintained, and each pull stays constant. Use the ideal model. Sliding friction equals limiting friction. Find the normal reaction and the limiting friction. Then find actual friction and acceleration in each trial. First, what does the coefficient tell us?

scenes.title: Actual friction can be below its limit

beats.text: Friction acts along the contact surface. Here it points left, opposing the box’s tendency to slide right, or its actual sliding to the right.
The coefficient, mu, depends on the two materials in contact. It has no units. Together with the normal reaction, it sets a limit.
The general rule is: actual friction f is less than or equal to mu R.
The maximum possible friction, f max, equals mu R. This is a ceiling, not the friction in every situation.
For example, before any pull, the box is at rest with only weight and reaction acting. There is no horizontal tendency to slide. Actual friction is zero.
As the pull grows, friction matches what is needed to keep the box at rest, up to its limit. Let’s calculate that limit.

scenes.title: First find the reaction and friction limit

beats.text: The pull is horizontal, and the box stays on the floor. Its vertical acceleration is zero, so the upward and downward forces balance.
Vertical resultant equals zero: reaction minus weight equals zero.
Therefore, reaction equals mass times g.
Substitute mass five and g ten. Reaction equals five times ten, which is fifty newtons.
Now use the limiting friction formula: f max equals mu R.
Zero point four times fifty gives a limiting friction of twenty newtons.
The floor can supply up to that much friction. It need not supply all of it. This same limit applies in every trial because the mass, surfaces and vertical forces stay the same.

scenes.title: Trials A and B: the box stays at rest

beats.text: Start trial A from rest. The twelve newton pull is below the twenty newton limit, so friction can balance the pull.
For equilibrium, pull minus friction equals zero.
So actual friction equals the pull: twelve newtons to the left.
To find acceleration, use resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Twelve minus twelve equals five a. Hence a is zero. Equal opposing forces give no acceleration.
Reset to rest for trial B. The twenty newton pull exactly equals the twenty newton friction limit.
This is limiting equilibrium: friction equals mu R, which is twenty newtons. The box is on the point of moving.
Again, resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
Twenty minus twenty equals five a, giving zero acceleration. Starting from rest, the box remains at rest, even at the limit.
Reaching the limit does not itself produce an unbalanced force. The pull must exceed it to start the box sliding.

scenes.title: Trial C: the pull exceeds the limit

beats.text: Reset the box to rest for trial C. Twenty five newtons exceeds the twenty newton limit. Friction cannot balance this pull.
The box begins sliding right. Under our model, friction now equals its limiting value: twenty newtons to the left.
Take right as positive. Newton’s second law is resultant force equals mass times acceleration.
The horizontal resultant is pull minus friction, so P minus f equals m a.
Substitute the pull, twenty five, friction, twenty, and mass, five.
The resultant is five newtons right. Dividing by five kilograms gives acceleration one metre per second squared, to the right.
Watch the box start from rest and cover more ground each second. The pull and friction remain constant, so its acceleration remains constant.

scenes.title: Check: rough does not mean maximum friction

beats.text: Return to trial A, starting from rest. What would change if we removed the pull altogether? Would friction still equal the twenty newton limit?
No. Actual friction would be zero. With no horizontal force tending to move the box, no friction is needed. The limit is still available.
Distinguish actual friction from its limit.
